title: Agastya's weapons
hook: before a great sage hands Rama new weapons, Sita asks whether he should be carrying weapons at all
carry: fire is kindled by being near fuel

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sharabhanga, part two. The old sage rose from the fire, the sages showed Rama the bones, and Rama promised to protect them, and your line, I'll protect you. Did you do one small thing within reach? Day five hundred fifty-seven.

They're walking between hermitages, Rama ahead with his bow, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind. The path is narrow, the trees are close, and nobody has spoken for a while. And Sita, quietly, starts to talk. She's been thinking about that promise. Not doubting Rama's goodness, she says. Worried about something else. You made a vow to kill the rakshasas, she says, and they haven't done anything to you. I'm afraid of what weapons do to the person who carries them.
screen: `SITA STARTS TO TALK.` → `THEY'VE DONE NOTHING TO YOU.` → `WHAT WEAPONS DO TO THEIR BEARER.`

segments.voice: Sita lays out her worry carefully. There are three faults that come from desire, she says. Speaking falsely. Wanting someone else's wife. And violence without any enmity, harming those who haven't harmed you. You've never done the first two. But the third worries me. And she tells him a story. Once there was an ascetic so devoted that Indra, king of the gods, grew uneasy. So Indra came disguised as a warrior and left a sword with him, asking him to keep it safe. The ascetic took the trust seriously. He carried the sword everywhere: to gather fruit, to bathe, to pray. Slowly, without noticing, he grew rough, then cruel, and lost his practice. Fire, she says, is kindled by being near fuel. Here in the forest, she says, let's live the forest's way. When we're home in Ayodhya, you can take up a warrior's duty again. And then she adds: I'm only saying this out of love. Rama's answer is just as tender. You say this because you care for me. But a warrior carries a bow so that no one in distress has to cry out unheard. The sages came to me for refuge. I gave my word. I could give up my life, he says, even you, even Lakshmana, sooner than a promise made to them. Two good people, two real concerns, and the text lets both speak. Then ten years pass, the text says, in the hermitages of Dandaka. And the road leads to the sage Rama has been told to seek: Agastya.
screen: `THREE FAULTS FROM DESIRE.` · `THE ASCETIC AND THE SWORD.` · `I SAY THIS OUT OF LOVE.` · `NO ONE CRIES OUT UNHEARD.` · then, large: `TWO GOOD PEOPLE, BOTH HEARD.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your hands rest empty in your lap. Notice what you usually carry: your phone, your keys, a worry, a grudge, a role. Name one of them silently. Then imagine setting it down beside you for these two minutes, not forever, just for now. Feel your hands without it. If it pulls at you, let it wait. Breathe, empty handed. The bell holds the time.
Agastya's weapons. Before the sage gives Rama weapons, Sita asks whether carrying them will change him, and Rama answers with his promise.
Your line: fire is kindled by being near fuel. Today, when someone you love questions you, answer as gently as they asked. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Reciters give Sita's question about weapons in the Aranya Kanda its full length, and Hindu teachers who discuss it note that the text lets both her concern and Rama's answer stand.

myth: she says he's free of falsehood; her worry is violence without enmity.
in Sita's story, Indra leaves a sword with an ascetic
carrying it everywhere slowly makes him cruel.

the text says Rama spends ten years among the sages.

fork.setup: you're Rama. Sita, out of love, asks you to set aside your vow to fight the rakshasas while in the forest. what do you say?
options: you're right, I'll give up the vow.
I gave my word to the sages; I can't take it back.
fork.reveal: Rama honors her concern, but says a promise to those who sought refuge is one he can't break.

original.note: Sanskrit agastya: the great sage of the south, whom Rama meets next.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama gets new weapons and that's that.
what it means: Sita first asks whether carrying weapons will change him.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 9–10 is a full dialogue: Sita's three faults and the sword parable, then Rama's answer about protecting those who seek refuge.
